input: Feedback control is best understood as a continuous conversation between a process and the equipment that watches over it, and a temperature loop on a process vessel offers a particularly clear window into that conversation. At the start of the loop stands the sensor, whose task is to observe the temperature of the material inside the vessel and to turn that observation into a signal that can travel onward. Without that signal, nothing else in the loop has anything to respond to, because the loop can only act on what it knows. The signal then reaches the controller, which compares the measured temperature with the desired temperature and considers not merely whether the two differ, but also the direction in which they differ. This comparison is the quiet decision point of the whole arrangement. Once the controller has formed its response, the instruction passes to the final element, the part of the loop that actually touches the process by changing the flow of heating or cooling medium that serves the vessel. It is at this point that information becomes action. Finally, the sign of the feedback completes the picture: the action taken is arranged to oppose the original deviation, so that a vessel growing hotter receives less heating effect, not more, and a vessel growing cooler receives more. The loop therefore works against its own error, repeatedly and patiently, which is precisely what makes it feedback rather than a one-way command passed down a chain. Each element, in other words, earns its place by what it hands to the next, and the chain is only as strong as the signal that travels along it from measurement to action.
target: A temperature loop on a process vessel has four parts in a fixed order: sensor, controller, final element, and the sign of the feedback. The sensor measures the temperature of the vessel contents and transmits the measurement as a signal. Measurement is the only information the loop holds; an unmeasured change in temperature produces no response until the sensor registers it. The controller receives the measurement and compares it with the set point, the desired temperature for the vessel contents. Comparison gives both the size of the error and its direction, and the controller sets its output from the two. The final element receives the controller output and changes the manipulated stream, the heating or cooling flow that serves the vessel. Action on the process occurs only at the final element; the sensor and the controller handle information alone. The sign of the feedback is negative. A temperature above the set point moves the final element to reduce the heating effect or increase the cooling effect, and a temperature below the set point moves the final element in the opposite direction. Each action opposes the deviation that produced it. The loop repeats the sequence continuously: measurement, comparison, action, and a further measurement of the changed temperature. The passage states structure only. No tuning values are given, and no response strength or speed follows from the structure alone. The order of the parts matters because each part depends on the part before it. A controller with no measurement has no error to answer, and a final element with no controller output has no instruction to follow. The sign completes the loop only when the action is arranged against the deviation; the same hardware joined with the opposite sign would drive the temperature away from the set point instead of toward it.
